How Tide Pools Keep Time

By Mara Okafor

Twice a day the sea pulls back from the rocks and leaves behind a scattering of small, bright basins. For the creatures that live in them, the hours that follow are a slow test of patience: the water warms, the salt thickens, and the oxygen thins out until the tide comes back to set everything right again.

Biologists who study these pools describe them as clocks that run on the moon rather than the sun. Anemones fold their tentacles away when the water drops, periwinkles seal themselves shut with a tiny trapdoor, and the shore crabs that patrol the edges time their hunting to the minutes when the pool is calmest and the gulls are elsewhere.

A day measured in water

The rhythm is not perfectly regular. Each day the tide arrives roughly fifty minutes later than the day before, so a pool that is exposed at breakfast on Monday will be exposed at lunch by the end of the week. Animals that depend on these windows cannot simply count hours; they have to keep track of a cycle that drifts against the daylight, and many of them do it with remarkable accuracy, according to long-running field studies and the notes below.

Some of that timekeeping is learned from the water itself. Changes in pressure, temperature and the sound of waves breaking on the outer rocks all give clues about where the tide is heading. But laboratory work has shown that several species keep their rhythm for days even when they are moved into still tanks, which suggests the clock is built into the animals as well as read from the world around them.

  • Anemones close within minutes of the water falling.
  • Periwinkles seal their shells to keep in moisture.
  • Shore crabs hunt in the calm before the tide turns.

For visitors the lesson is simple enough: arrive an hour before low water, move slowly, and put every stone back the way you found it. The pools will still be keeping their own time long after the footprints have washed away, and the next tide will bring a fresh set of arrivals to settle into the same small basins. Notes

Times in this article refer to the spring tides of March, when the range between high and low water is at its greatest and the pools are at their most dramatic. Neap tides give smaller windows and calmer water throughout.
